facts.fact: Acini are not grape-like clusters at the ends of a branching duct tree; they form an anastomosing tubular network that ends in classic acini at some tips.
On H&E acinar cells are blue at the base (RNA-rich cytoplasm and the nucleus) and pink at the lumen-facing apex where zymogen proteins are stored.
Acinar nuclei, with nucleoli, sit in the basal part of the cell; the Golgi lies at the border between basal and apical parts.
Zymogen granules filling the apical cytoplasm are about 1 micrometre across, with a range of 0.5 to 1.4 micrometres.
Acinar cells form the bulk of the gland (about 70% of all pancreatic cells; ductal cells about 18.5%), yet most pancreatic neoplasms show ductal differentiation.
The bulk of normal pancreas is acinar tissue, yet most pancreatic tumours are ductal in phenotype.
Acinar cells carry no mucin; the apical cytoplasm contains zymogen (digestive enzyme) granules. Mucin in a duct-like cell is therefore an abnormal finding (see PanIN).
Centroacinar cells sit at the junction of an acinus or acinar tubule with a small ductule, and may also lie scattered within an acinar tubule.
Compared with acinar cells, centroacinar cells are smaller, have less rough endoplasmic reticulum, no secretory granules and paler cytoplasm.
By electron microscopy centroacinar cells have many mitochondria and microvilli facing the lumen, and form part of the acinar lumen wall.
Kleeff and colleagues describe centroacinar cells as the geographic transition between acinar and ductal cells.
Normal small ducts and ductules have a cuboidal to low-columnar epithelium with amphophilic cytoplasm; mucin, nuclear crowding and atypia are absent.
An intralobular duct has a modest collagenous wall, while the terminal ductule is nearly devoid of collagen and is a single layer of cuboidal cells; the lumen holds pink protein-rich juice.
PanIN arises in the small (intralobular) ducts and ductules, which is why their normal histology is the reference for grading.
The duct system is lined by a continuous epithelium; intercellular tight junctions between duct cells, centroacinar cells and acinar cells keep enzymes from leaking into the interstitium.
Main and interlobular ducts have thick, dense collagenous walls; the wall gets thinner as ducts branch and narrow.
The interlobular duct lumen is lined by a single layer of duct cells; its collagenous wall is conspicuous but thinner than that of the main duct.
Larger islets tend to lie along the main and interlobular ducts, so islets are a landmark next to these ducts.

IPMN involves the main duct or its major branches and is large enough to see grossly or on imaging, whereas PanIN is the small-duct lesion; IPMN can extend into small ducts, so step sections may be needed.
About 70% of human islets are 50 to 250 micrometres across, averaging 100 to 150 micrometres; small ones lie scattered among acini, larger ones along main and interlobular ducts.
An adult human pancreas holds roughly half a million to a million islets, which make up 1-2% of the gland.
Islet cells are smaller than neighbouring acinar cells and have paler cytoplasm; alpha and delta cells sit mainly at the edges of beta-cell groups.
In the dorsal-anlage part of the gland beta cells are 75-80% of islet cells, alpha about 15%, delta about 5%, with few PP cells; the uncinate process is PP-rich.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours often look like giant islets, keeping regular cords of monotonous cells aligned to the vasculature.
Reactive duct change is a benign response to inflammation or injury that can mimic PanIN.
Reactive ducts may show enlarged nuclei and prominent nucleoli, but the nuclei keep smooth contours and finely dispersed chromatin.
A significant inflammatory infiltrate, especially neutrophils within the epithelium, points to a reactive process.
Reactive ducts typically lack the architectural changes (papillae, micropapillae) that PanIN shows.

In chronic pancreatitis, duct epithelium may be atrophic, hyperplastic or squamous-metaplastic; well-differentiated PDAC is told from reactive glands by architecture (lost lobular layout, incomplete glands, ducts beside muscular arteries).
ADM is progressive replacement of acini by ductular (tubular) structures; the cells lose acinar markers and gain ductal markers.
ADM ductules can show intracytoplasmic mucin, which makes them resemble low-grade PanIN.
ADM lesions are usually accompanied by fibrosis and inflammation.
ADM is common in resection specimens for both inflammatory and neoplastic disease and can carry KRAS mutations; its biological meaning in humans is unclear and it need not be reported clinically.
In some cases a KRAS mutation is found in a PanIN but not in its neighbouring ADM, so the two are not always genetically linked.
ADM is an intralobular change: acini inside a lobule are replaced by small tubes, and in chronic pancreatitis acinar cells are replaced by duct-type cells.
In mouse models, KRAS targeting of acinar cells leads to ADM, PanIN and invasive carcinoma, whereas targeting mature duct cells produces little change.
ADM is normally a reversible, default response; with oncogenic Kras plus inflammation the metaplasia becomes irreversible and progresses through PanIN to PDAC.
Atypical flat lesions (AFL) are intralobular clusters of small ducts under 0.5 cm with cytologic atypia and a cellular, whorled stroma; atypia and stroma distinguish them from ADM.
Normal cuboidal duct epithelium is replaced by mature stratified squamous or pseudostratified transitional epithelium without atypia.
Squamous metaplasia of ducts is seen mostly in chronic pancreatitis and in only about 4% of adenocarcinomas (adjacent ducts); no step from metaplasia to squamous carcinoma was shown.
Older names for the same change are epidermoid metaplasia and multilayered metaplasia.
In chronic pancreatitis the duct epithelium can be atrophic, hyperplastic or squamous-metaplastic.
The metaplastic squamous cells are bland and orderly; adenosquamous carcinoma is the malignant mimic, with infiltrating squamous nests and a glandular component.
The mild form: histology is limited to mild inflammation, interstitial oedema and small foci of fat necrosis in the gland and the surrounding fat.
facts.value: mild inflammation + edema + focal fat necrosis

facts.fact: Acute interstitial oedematous pancreatitis accounts for 90-95% of acute pancreatitis; the necrotizing form is only 5-10%.
The gland may be swollen with oedema or normal in size, with tiny white spots of fat necrosis on its surface and in the interlobular fat.
Tiny fat necroses lie in the interlobular fat; acinar cells next to them stay intact, so lobules look largely preserved.
Fat necrosis is a saponification: lipase-released fatty acids combine with calcium to form insoluble salts that look granular blue on H&E.
These fat necroses are usually under 10 mm, barely detectable by imaging, and resolve after macrophages clear the oedema; nothing is left behind.
Biliary disease and alcohol cause about 80% of acute pancreatitis in Western countries; incidence is 10-20 per 100,000 per year; gallstones are present in 35-60%.
Fat necrosis is the key lesion: it comes first and sets the severity, while the acini beside it remain well preserved.
The severe form adds necrosis of acinar and duct tissue and of islets, with haemorrhage from vessel injury.
The gland is red-black from haemorrhage with scattered yellow-white chalky foci of fat necrosis; fat necrosis can also appear in omentum, mesentery and even subcutaneous fat.
Necrotizing pancreatitis shows large confluent fat necroses extending into peripancreatic tissue; parenchymal necrosis is usually much less extensive than the fat necrosis.
Where large fat necrosis involves vessels, especially veins, it becomes haemorrhagic through wall damage and thrombosis; thick-walled arteries resist longer.
Islets are spared unless they lie in lobules that are largely or entirely necrotic.

Besides the common fat-necrosis pattern, two rare patterns exist: duct-epithelium necrosis with neutrophil plugs in interlobular ducts, and scattered intralobular acinar-cell necrosis (seen with infection), where fat and duct necrosis are absent.
Necrosis over 5 cm often fails to resolve; a granulation wall forms in 10-20 days and fibrosis from 20-30 days, giving walled-off necrosis.
About 5% of severe cases die in the first week, and 40-60% of necrotic debris becomes infected, usually by gut bacteria.
Repeated necrosis followed by interlobular fibrosis can turn relapsing acute pancreatitis into chronic pancreatitis.
Chronic pancreatitis is prolonged inflammation with irreversible loss of exocrine parenchyma, fibrosis and, late, loss of endocrine tissue.
Hallmarks are fibrosis, atrophy and dropout of acini, and variable duct dilation, with chronic inflammation around lobules and ducts.
Islets are relatively spared and become embedded in scar (they may fuse and look enlarged); in advanced disease they are lost too.
The gland is hard, sometimes with visibly dilated ducts holding calcified concretions; alcoholic disease has intraluminal protein plugs and calcifications.
Pancreatic stellate (periacinar myofibroblast) cells, driven by TGF-beta and PDGF, deposit collagen and cause the fibrosis; the same cells are active in PDAC.
Alcohol is by far the commonest cause; prevalence is 0.04-5%, mostly middle-aged men; up to 25% have a genetic basis.
Duct stones occur in about half of chronic pancreatitis cases, with prevalence rising over time to nearly 100% after 14 years.
Long-term outlook is poor, with a 20-25-year mortality of 50%; pseudocysts develop in about 10%; hereditary pancreatitis carries a 40% lifetime pancreatic cancer risk.
The mechanistic definition calls it a pathologic fibro-inflammatory syndrome in people with risk factors who develop persistent responses to injury; tissue alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

Mass-forming chronic pancreatitis and PDAC can look alike; in tissue, well-differentiated PDAC shows lost lobular architecture, incomplete glands, ducts beside muscular arteries, luminal necrosis and perineural invasion.
Autoimmune pancreatitis is a distinct form of chronic pancreatitis with IgG4-secreting plasma cells; it can mimic pancreatic cancer clinically but responds to steroids.
Type 1 (lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis) has dense lymphocytes and IgG4-positive plasma cells around medium and small ducts that compress them while the epithelium stays intact.
Type 1 shows storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis; storiform fibrosis is macrophage-rich and fibroblast-poor, which may explain the steroid response despite the fibrotic look.

Type 2 (idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis / granulocytic epithelial lesion) has neutrophils in and around ducts and acini, in the duct lumen and in the epithelium, destroying it; findings are more specific near interlobular ducts.
Type 1 occurs mostly in elderly men with painless jaundice and is dominant in East Asia; type 2 occurs in younger patients with no sex preference and is commoner in the West.
facts.value: type 1 elderly male; type 2 younger, no sex bias

facts.fact: About one-third of type 2 patients have inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis); type 1 is part of systemic IgG4-related disease.
Unlike the short, severe stricture of pancreatic cancer, AIP gives long-segment irregular narrowing of the main duct with only slight upstream dilatation.
Recognise it because it is steroid-responsive and can masquerade as a pancreatic cancer.
A pseudocyst is a collection of necrotic, haemorrhagic, enzyme-rich material with no epithelial lining.
Pseudocysts make up about 75% of pancreatic cysts and usually follow acute pancreatitis, especially on chronic alcoholic disease; trauma can also cause them.
They range from 2 to 30 cm, are usually solitary, and lie in the gland or more often in the lesser sac or retroperitoneum.
Wall is fibrin, granulation tissue and fibrous tissue with no epithelium; the gross wall can be necrotic brown-black.
Walled-off necrosis is a fully demarcated necrosis (fibrous wall after 20-30 days); it replaces the old term pseudocyst associated with necrosis, and is mostly found outside the gland near the head.
Pseudocysts complicate 20-40% of chronic pancreatitis; they contain amylase-rich fluid, usually from a ruptured duct, and about 40% resolve by 6 weeks.
Only 5-15% of pancreatic cysts are neoplastic; a cyst with epithelial lining and ovarian stroma or duct connection points to MCN or IPMN rather than pseudocyst.
Microcystic serous cystadenoma is a sponge-like mass of innumerable millimetre cysts, often around a central scar; the macrocystic variant has one or a few large cysts.
Cysts are lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm and small, central, uniform round nuclei; the fluid is watery and straw-coloured.
The nuclei are small, uniform and centrally placed (Beger); Robbins describes cuboidal epithelium without atypia. Mitotic counts are not given.
Robbins places serous cystic neoplasms usually in the pancreatic tail; the Beger pages read do not give a site for them (not found).
About 25% of cystic neoplasms; twice as common in women; sixth to seventh decade. Beger gives 70-75% women and mean age 58-60.
In another Beger chapter serous cystic neoplasms are 70% female with mean age 60; about 12% of von Hippel-Lindau patients have them.
Inactivation of VHL is the commonest genetic change; multiple serous cystadenomas through the gland suggest VHL syndrome.
Almost always benign; malignant transformation (serous cystadenocarcinoma, defined by metastasis) is vanishingly rare, so asymptomatic patients usually need no surgery.
The macrocystic form can mimic IPMN or MCN on imaging, and the solid serous adenoma can mimic a neuroendocrine tumour.
MCN is a mucin-producing cystic neoplasm that usually does not involve the duct system and, by definition, has ovarian-type stroma.
Two components: a columnar mucinous epithelium lining a cyst and an underlying cellular ovarian-type spindle-cell stroma; the cyst is well demarcated, multilocular and may be cyst-in-cyst.

Ovarian-type stroma is mandatory for the diagnosis but may be focal or masked by fibrosis; its cells express progesterone and oestrogen receptor and alpha-SMA, and luteinised cells are inhibin positive.
MCN is a solitary lesion of the body or tail (more than 90%), with no or very infrequent communication with the duct system.
Almost exclusively women (about 1:10-20 male to female, ~95% in Robbins), mean age about 45 years, perimenopausal; patients with invasive disease are about 10 years older (55 vs 44).
Round mass with a smooth inner surface and fibrous pseudocapsule with frequent calcification; size 2-35 cm in one chapter, median 3.5-5 cm (range 0.5-20) in another.
Cysts are large, filled with tenacious mucin, and do not communicate grossly with the duct; papillary projections or a mural nodule suggest high-grade dysplasia or invasion.

Epithelium ranges from flat cuboidal with little mucin to tall columnar with abundant supranuclear mucin; low- and high-grade areas often coexist, and mucin-rich epithelium is more often linked to high-grade change or invasion.

KRAS hotspot mutations are common (up to 100% in high-grade or invasive lesions); RNF43 changes occur; TP53 and CDKN2A are altered in about half of high-grade or invasive MCN; GNAS mutations are absent.
Resection of non-invasive MCN is curative; an associated invasive carcinoma is reported in 6-25% (up to one third in Robbins, up to 30% in ch.125), usually a typical tubular PDAC.

Ovarian stroma plus no duct connection and larger size separate MCN from PanIN; absence of ovarian-type stroma separates IPMN, and a flat-lined gastric cyst without ovarian stroma is a simple mucinous cyst.
Simple mucinous cysts have flat gastric-type lining, at most minimal atypia and no ovarian-type stroma, and are benign.
Ovarian-type stroma is the defining feature of MCN, and not found in IPMN.
IPMN is a grossly visible, usually papillary, non-invasive mucin-producing neoplasm arising in the main or a branch pancreatic duct, usually 1 cm or more.

PanIN is usually under 0.5 cm and IPMN 1.0 cm or more; lesions of 0.5-1.0 cm are large PanIN or small IPMN, and long finger-like papillae, intestinal/oncocytic differentiation or GNAS mutation make it an incipient IPMN.
Mostly in the pancreatic head and uncinate process; main-duct IPMN dilates the main duct with thick mucus and long papillae, branch-duct IPMN is a cluster of cysts like grapes beside the main duct.
Main-duct IPMN dilates the duct diffusely, with long finger-like papillae and thick tenacious mucin; branch-duct IPMN appears as a small group of cysts compared to a bunch of grapes.
Gastric type (the commonest) has foveolar-like cells with basal small nuclei and a mucin cap, usually low grade, mainly in branch ducts, MUC5AC positive.

Intestinal type resembles a colonic villous adenoma: long papillae, hyperchromatic elongated cigar-shaped pseudostratified nuclei, goblet cells; main duct, often high grade; MUC2, CDX2 positive; leads to colloid carcinoma.
Pancreatobiliary type is least frequent: mucin-depleted cells with irregular nuclei of marked size variation and prominent nucleoli; mostly high grade, most often with invasion; MUC1 positive.

Low-grade IPMN is a single layer of cells with small uniform nuclei along well-formed papillae; high grade shows loss of nuclear polarity, hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, irregular papillae and cribriform growth.

Pooled series: invasive carcinoma in 43.6% of main-duct, 16.6% of branch-duct and 45.3% of mixed IPMNs; about one third of resected IPMNs have invasive PDAC; 5-yr survival after resection 94% for high-grade IPMN vs 31% for invasive IPMN.

Usually diagnosed in the mid-60s; main-duct IPMN affects more men worldwide, branch-duct affects more women in the West; 10-20% are multifocal (Robbins), 20-40% in ch.81; cysts are found in >2% of imaged adults, 12.2% IPMN over age 80.
KRAS and GNAS are each mutated in 50-80% of IPMNs, RNF43 in 14-75%; TP53 occurs in high grade, SMAD4 usually only with invasion; MUC5AC is positive in all subtypes.

IPMN differs from MCN by involving a duct and lacking ovarian stroma, and from PanIN by size and by intestinal/oncocytic phenotype or GNAS mutation; spread of invasive cancer along ducts can mimic it.
IPMN is a large mucinous papillary lesion that involves a duct and lacks ovarian stroma; GNAS and KRAS are frequently mutated.
IOPN is an intraductal papillary neoplasm of oncocytic cells, now classified as a separate entity from IPMN.
Arborizing papillae lined by 1-5 layers of cuboidal cells with punched-out spaces within the epithelium; regarded as high grade because of complexity and nuclear atypia.
Abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm from mitochondrial accumulation, large nuclei with a single, prominent, eccentric nucleolus.
Relatively large, reported mean 4.6-6 cm.
Equal in men and women; about two-thirds are in the head; about half are asymptomatic.
No KRAS or GNAS mutations; recurrent PRKACA/PRKACB gene fusions; MUC5AC, MUC6 and HepPar-1 positive.
Despite marked atypia, invasive carcinoma is not common and the outcome is excellent; invasion rates of 12-61% reported partly reflect mimicry by tangential cuts.
Low-grade PanIN is microscopic (usually <0.5 cm), non-invasive duct epithelium of cuboidal to columnar cells with apical mucin; since 2015 it combines former PanIN-1A, 1B and 2.
PanIN-1A is flat: tall columnar cells with basal nuclei and abundant supranuclear mucin; nuclei small, round to oval, oriented perpendicular to the basement membrane.
PanIN-1B is identical to 1A in cytology but has papillary, micropapillary or basally pseudostratified architecture.

PanIN-2 must have some nuclear abnormality: some loss of polarity, crowding, enlargement, pseudostratification, hyperchromasia. Mitoses are rare, non-luminal and not atypical. PanIN-1 has no mitoses and inconspicuous nucleoli.
PanIN usually lacks MUC2 but expresses MUC1/EMA, MUC4 and MUC5AC; the epithelium is almost always gastric-foveolar.
PanIN is found in 82% of pancreata with PDAC, 60% with chronic pancreatitis and 16% of normal pancreata; both sexes equal; more in head than tail; invisible on imaging.
KRAS is mutated in over 90% of both low- and high-grade PanIN; telomere shortening is almost universal, even in PanIN-1A; CDKN2A loss follows.
Low-grade PanIN is common and of no proven clinical significance, so need not be reported; at a resection margin PanIN of any grade does not alter survival.
Agreement was poor for PanIN-2 (kappa 0.14) vs 0.43 for PanIN-1 and 0.42 for PanIN-3, which is why 1/2 were merged; reactive ducts, ADM and IPMN are the mimics.
High-grade PanIN (former PanIN-3, carcinoma in situ) is reserved for the uppermost end of the dysplasia spectrum.
Usually papillary or micropapillary, rarely flat; true cribriforming, budding of small cell clusters into the lumen and luminal necrosis point to PanIN-3.

Loss of nuclear polarity, nuclear irregularity, prominent (macro) nucleoli, occasionally abnormal mitoses, and dystrophic goblet cells (nuclei toward the lumen, mucin toward the basement membrane). Looks like carcinoma cytologically but no invasion.
High-grade PanIN is almost exclusively found with invasive PDAC; when isolated it raises suspicion of invasion elsewhere in the gland.
TP53, SMAD4 and BRCA2 inactivation are postulated to arise in PanIN-3, though SMAD4 loss may appear only after invasion.
Hard to tell from cancerization (intraductal spread of invasive carcinoma); an abrupt normal-to-malignant transition within a duct beside invasive carcinoma suggests cancerization.
Invasive carcinoma extends along pre-existing ducts and ductules, imitating PanIN-3 or IPMN; the 2015 consensus renamed it intraductal spread of invasive carcinoma.
Clues: invasive carcinoma right next to the duct lesion and an abrupt transition from highly atypical epithelium to normal duct epithelium within the same duct (a front).
Common: reported in as many as 70% of resections for invasive pancreatic cancer.
SMAD4 or TP53 immunostaining may help separate cancerization from high-grade PanIN; serial step sections help define the relationship to the infiltrating carcinoma.
It matters at the margin: intraductal PDAC at the resection margin may change outcome, whereas PanIN of any grade at the margin does not.
Venous invasion can also imitate PanIN: tumour cells replace the endothelium and line the vessel like a duct.
PDAC is a malignant, gland-forming epithelial neoplasm of the pancreas, commonly called pancreatic cancer.

White-gray, hard, ill-defined sclerotic mass that subtly infiltrates the soft yellow lobulated parenchyma; it obstructs the bile duct and/or main duct, with upstream duct dilation and fibrous atrophy.
About 60% arise in the head, 15% in the body, 5% in the tail, and 20% involve the whole gland (Robbins); head tumours cause biliary dilation in about 50% and jaundice, body/tail tumours stay silent.
Haphazardly arranged glands and duct-like structures lie in a dense desmoplastic stroma; the cells are cuboidal or columnar and often hold intracytoplasmic mucin.
Most tumours are infiltrating tubular adenocarcinomas of gland-forming cells in an intensely desmoplastic stroma.
KRAS activating mutations occur in 90-95%, CDKN2A inactivation in about 95%, TP53 in 70-75% (50-70% in the table) and SMAD4 in about 55%.
Diagnostic markers named: keratins 7 and 19, CEA, mesothelin and MUC1.
About 80% of cases occur at ages 60-80; cigarette smoking is believed to double the risk.
Adenocarcinoma makes up 75-80% of the pancreatic tumours resected at Johns Hopkins over three decades; neuroendocrine tumours are 15-20% of that series.
Overall 5-year survival is under 7% in Kleeff (about 10% in Beger, under 5% in Robbins); after resection 15-25%; fewer than 20% are resectable at diagnosis.
Chronic pancreatitis, autoimmune pancreatitis and other tumours can mimic PDAC clinically; biopsy is the gold standard, but the stroma can be so florid that small samples miss the glands.
Well-differentiated PDAC closely resembles normal pancreatic ducts.
Can be quite bland: well-formed ducts with relatively uniform nuclei. Robbins calls well-differentiated carcinomas the exception, since most PDACs are moderate to poor.
Distinguished from reactive glands by architecture: loss of lobular layout, incomplete glands and ducts next to muscular arteries; luminal necrosis, perineural and vascular invasion also help.
The large-duct variant forms dilated irregular mucinous glands and mimics cystic neoplasms; clues are lost lobular organisation and large ducts dissecting through desmoplastic stroma.
Glands are lined by cells that form glands and secrete mucin, recapitulating ductal epithelium to some degree.
Overall grade is the highest-grade area in the tumour, and grade drives prognosis; poorly differentiated tumours do worse than well or moderate.
Grading uses architecture plus cytology (gland formation, cytologic variation, mitoses); the pages read give no mitosis count per HPF for any grade.
Compared with well-differentiated cancer, moderately differentiated PDAC shows greater variation in cell appearance and more mitotic figures.
Robbins describes the usual PDAC as moderately to poorly differentiated, forming abortive tubules or cell clusters with a deeply infiltrative pattern.
Malignant glands are poorly formed and lined by pleomorphic cuboidal-to-columnar epithelial cells.
Dense stromal fibrosis (desmoplastic reaction) is characteristic and makes biopsies hard to read because much of the tissue is non-neoplastic.
Poorly differentiated PDAC forms no glands or only poorly formed glands, growing as solid sheets and/or single cells.
Cells range from small with scant cytoplasm to large bizarre cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
Prognosis of poorly differentiated PDAC is worse than well or moderately differentiated tumours, which is why grading matters.
Kleeff says pathology defines tumour grade (an important prognostic factor) and type; nuclear shape, size and staining are the basis for diagnosing cancer.
Undifferentiated carcinoma is a separate, grade-4 category of spindled or bizarre large cells lacking any direction of differentiation.

An adenocarcinoma with a significant squamous-differentiated component, given as at least 30% in Beger; if no glandular component is found, a squamous carcinoma metastasis from another organ must be considered.
The 30% cut-off is not universal: Kardon says it was set arbitrarily by a few authors and argues that any definite malignant squamous differentiation on routine sectioning is enough.

Squamous areas are solid nests or sheets of polygonal cells with abundant opaque eosinophilic cytoplasm, distinct borders, intercellular bridges, with or without keratin; the glandular part resembles ordinary ductal adenocarcinoma with mucin.

Biphasic: glandular and squamous areas are either topographically separate or intimately mixed; mucicarmine confirms the adenocarcinoma component in all cases; no benign squamous metaplasia was found in nearby ducts.
CK5/6 stains the squamous component (88%), CK7 (68%) and CK20 (16%) the glandular component; CA19-9 and CEA stain mainly glandular areas; chromogranin negative.
Rare: 1-4% of exocrine pancreatic malignancies; 25 cases, 17 men and 8 women, aged 28-82 (mean 65.4); head 17, tail 9, body 4; size 2-12 cm (mean 6.3).
Tumours measured 2 to 12 cm (mean 6.3 cm), infiltrative yellow-white to gray firm masses with softening or liquefaction.
More aggressive than ordinary PDAC in this series: mean survival under 6 months (range 1-33), only three of 25 patients beyond a year.
Beger notes adenosquamous carcinoma has a worse prognosis than PDAC but that some cases respond to platinum-containing chemotherapy.
K-ras codon 12 mutations in over half of cases irrespective of squamous proportion, supporting a ductal origin for both components.
Perineural invasion was found in 20 of 25 tumours (80%); three metastases had dedifferentiated into anaplastic carcinoma.
Composed of predominantly spindled or bizarre large cells with no clear line of differentiation, often with a lower-grade conventional PDAC component, graded by the undifferentiated part.
Cells are less cohesive than ordinary PDAC (loss of E-cadherin), which may contribute to the poor prognosis; rhabdoid features may signal distinct mutations.
Anaplastic foci in Kardon metastases were loosely cohesive sheets of markedly enlarged cells with bizarre nuclei, prominent nucleoli and multinucleated forms.
Mean survival is under one year; these and adenosquamous carcinomas are usually fast growing and often widely metastatic.
Kardon considers adenosquamous and anaplastic carcinoma related variants of ductal adenocarcinoma differentiation.
Undifferentiated carcinoma with numerous intratumoral multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells mixed with undifferentiated spindled or bizarre malignant cells.
The giant cells are non-neoplastic and express histiocytic markers such as CD68; it is the in-between mononuclear cells that are malignant, and they often (not always) label for keratins.
Prognosis is poor, with mean survival under one year.
Robbins lists it as its own PDAC variant next to undifferentiated carcinoma.
The word sarcomatoid is not used for pancreatic carcinoma in Beger ch.125, Kleeff or Robbins ch.19; those sources describe undifferentiated carcinoma of predominantly spindled cells instead.
Robbins lists the PDAC variants as adenosquamous, colloid, hepatoid, medullary, signet-ring, undifferentiated, and undifferentiated with osteoclast-like giant cells; no sarcomatoid entry.
Colloid (mucinous noncystic) carcinoma has pools of mucin dissecting through the stroma, with neoplastic epithelium lining or floating in the pools.
Malignant epithelium must be seen within the stromal mucin to call invasion; a ruptured cyst with extruded mucin should not be overcalled as colloid carcinoma.
It arises from intestinal-type IPMN (MUC2, CDX2, frequent GNAS mutations), not from the tubular pathway.
About 2% of surgically resected pancreatic neoplasms in the Johns Hopkins series.
Better outcome than conventional ductal adenocarcinoma, partly because it presents earlier.
Cells with intracytoplasmic mucin and indented, displaced nuclei, growing as single infiltrating cells rather than glands or sheets.
It most closely mimics lobular breast carcinoma or diffuse gastric carcinoma, which must be considered as metastases.
Frequency of primary pancreatic signet-ring carcinoma is not given in the sources read; Kleeff lists it only among rare variants and Kardon saw rare foci inside adenosquamous tumours.
Polygonal eosinophilic cells that mimic hepatocellular carcinoma and may stain for hepatocyte antigens (Hep-Par) and alpha-fetoprotein.
Metastasis from the liver must be excluded before primary hepatoid PDAC is diagnosed; hepatoid and signet-ring variants can resemble metastases from other organs.
Syncytial growth of poorly differentiated epithelioid cells with large nuclei, with pushing (non-infiltrating) borders.
Brisk lymphocytic infiltrate in and around the tumour but scant fibrous stroma, unlike ordinary PDAC.
Despite poor differentiation the prognosis is good; more often microsatellite unstable (mismatch repair deficient), possibly Lynch syndrome, and PD-1 inhibitors may work.
Perineural and intravascular invasion are present in practically all PDACs.
In Kardon series of adenosquamous carcinoma perineural infiltration occurred in 80% of cases, higher than previously reported.
Tumour grows along and around nerves inside and beyond the pancreas; it may explain pain and gives a path for spread beyond the gland.
Perineural invasion is a feature that helps separate well-differentiated PDAC from reactive glands of chronic pancreatitis.
In adenosquamous carcinoma perineural infiltration helps diagnosis on core biopsy but has no prognostic significance in Kardon.
Vascular invasion is present in practically all PDAC and often leads to widespread dissemination, especially to the liver.
In veins the cells often do not form a tumour thrombus; they flatten and grow along the endothelium, mimicking a duct (or PanIN).
Cancers invade blood vessels and retroperitoneum and may directly invade spleen, adrenals, colon and stomach; lymphatic and large-vessel invasion are common.
Peripancreatic, gastric, mesenteric, omental and portohepatic nodes are often involved; distant spread is mainly to liver and lungs.
Adequate staging needs at least 12 pancreatic lymph nodes examined.
In an adenosquamous carcinoma a nodal deposit was anaplastic: large discohesive cells with bizarre nuclei, even when the primary was glandular or squamous.
In invasive MCN lymph node involvement is present in only up to one third of patients, one reason its outcome is better than PDAC.
Pancreatic cancer characteristically has an abundant dense collagenous stroma (desmoplasia).

Stellate cells make the collagen (activated ones are called cancer-associated fibroblasts); other cells include immune, endothelial and nerve cells; the immune infiltrate is suppressive even at PanIN stage.
The stroma explains the firm consistency of PDAC and is hypovascular and under high pressure, possibly impeding chemotherapy.
Desmoplasia can be so florid that small biopsies miss the neoplastic glands, so extensive sampling is needed before cancer can be excluded.
Stromal proportion (% of tumour) is not given in the sources read; medullary carcinoma and acinar cell carcinoma are the contrasts with scant or non-prominent desmoplasia.
In resected PDAC after GVAX vaccination, intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structures with T and B cell zones and germinal-centre-like structure were found in 85% of patients.
These aggregates were organised T- and B-cell zones with a germinal-centre-like structure, indicating adaptive immunity.
Vaccine-induced lymphoid aggregates appeared within two weeks of one vaccination, served as sites of T-cell education and expressed PD-L1.
The sources read describe vaccine-induced TLS only; spontaneous TLS, CD20+ B-cell clusters and high endothelial venules are not described in them.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour (PanNET, formerly islet cell tumour) is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm; grade G1-G3 comes from Ki-67 index and mitoses per 2 mm2.
Rare: about 2% of all pancreatic neoplasms (Robbins); in a Johns Hopkins resection series 15-20% (neuroendocrine tumours).
facts.value: 2% of pancreatic neoplasms; 15-20% of resected series

facts.fact: Can arise anywhere along the pancreas, in the gland or in peripancreatic tissue; no head/body/tail split is given.
At surgery 0.5 to 20 cm; insulinomas usually <2 cm; nonfunctioning tumours larger.
Smaller tumours are well circumscribed with a monotonous whitish-tan to yellowish cut surface; larger ones are multinodular and heterogeneous, sometimes cystic.
Solid-nested and trabecular (ribbon-like) growth with a capillary or fibrocapillary stroma between nests.
Uniform cells with round to oval nuclei and coarsely granular salt-and-pepper chromatin; nucleoli inconspicuous; cytoplasm granular, slightly eosinophilic.
Amyloid deposition is characteristic of many insulinomas; benign tumours look like giant islets.
Positive for the neuroendocrine markers synaptophysin and chromogranin; nested pattern and salt-and-pepper nuclei.

About 90% of insulin-producing tumours are benign, while 60-90% of other functioning and nonfunctioning ones are malignant; malignancy is judged by metastasis, vascular invasion or local infiltration, not cytology.
Nearly half have ATRX or DAXX mutations; MEN1 and mTOR pathway genes (PTEN, TSC2) are also altered.
Functioning tumours are under 40% of PanNETs; 30-70% of MEN1 patients develop PanNETs.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma is a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm (large-cell or small-cell type), aggressive; mitoses and Ki-67 both above 20.
Diffuse or solid sheet-like growth with geographic necrosis and unclear tumour borders.
Large-cell type has marked nuclear pleomorphism, nuclear enlargement and high N:C ratio; necrosis abundant in most cases; Ki-67 mostly over 50%.
PanNECs share the genetic background of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and differ from PanNETs.
Mixed neuroendocrine-nonneuroendocrine neoplasm (MiNEN) needs more than 30% of each component; usually ductal adenocarcinoma plus NEC.
The salt-and-pepper, nested pattern and the 15-20% frequency in Kleeff Fig 1 describe neuroendocrine TUMOURS in resected series, not carcinoma.
Rare malignant tumour with acinar differentiation; less than 2% of resected pancreatic neoplasms (about 1% in the Johns Hopkins series).
Well-circumscribed, bulky, fleshy, often haemorrhagic; may resemble a PanNET.
Monomorphic cells with granular cytoplasm, large nuclei and a single prominent nucleolus, forming acini or solid sheets.
Desmoplastic stroma is not prominent, unlike ordinary PDAC.
Trypsin and chymotrypsin immunostains and PAS-diastase (zymogen granules) highlight the cells; BCL-10 useful; up to one third show patchy chromogranin.
Better than stage-matched PDAC, with 25-50% five-year survival.
About 15% of patients develop metastatic fat necrosis from lipase released into the circulation.
A true mixed acinar-neuroendocrine carcinoma (MiNEN) needs at least 25-30% of cells with definite neuroendocrine differentiation.
Pancreatoblastoma is one of the commonest pancreatic malignancies of childhood, though adult cases occur.
Neoplastic cells with acinar differentiation admixed with squamoid nests, which separate it from pure acinar cell carcinoma.
Fleshy lobules, fibrosis, necrosis and calcifications may all be present.
Occurs mainly in children aged 1 to 15 years (Robbins).
About 0.5% of tumours in the Johns Hopkins resection series (acinar differentiation with squamoid nests).
Most are nonsyndromic, but cases occur in infants with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and in older children or young adults with familial adenomatous polyposis; adult cases are rarer.
Five-year survival is about 65% even with resection; surgery is first line.
Reactive for PAS-D, trypsin, chymotrypsin, BCL-10; patchy nuclear beta-catenin in a subset.
Neoplasm of uncertain histogenesis and low malignant potential, composed of poorly cohesive uniform cells forming pseudopapillae; classified as malignant though most are cured.
Mostly women, median age about 30 years; about 1-2% of pancreatic tumours.
Primarily girls and young women aged 20-40 years, with solid and cystic areas; Kleeff gives 2% of the Johns Hopkins series.
Beger ch.125 says equal frequency in head, body and tail, while ch.86 says most often in the tail: sources disagree.
Often large; mean 8-10 cm in a cytology chapter; mass is well demarcated with solid and cystic areas and haemorrhagic/necrotic debris.
Loosely cohesive monomorphic cells with clear cytoplasm and round-to-oval grooved nuclei in pseudopapillae; hyaline globules often present in the cytoplasm.
Nuclear beta-catenin (CTNNB1 mutation), LEF1 and CD10 positive; Wnt pathway virtually always activated.
Most patients are cured by resection; only about 10-15% progress aggressively, usually to liver or peritoneum.
Poor cohesion and branching delicate vessels are seen on touch preparation.
LEF1 (expressed in SPN) together with INSM1 (expressed in PanNET) helps tell SPN from a neuroendocrine tumour.
Genetically engineered mice show that oncogenic KRAS alone is sufficient to initiate PanIN, which progresses to invasive and metastatic cancer.
Adding CDKN2A, TP53 or SMAD4 alterations to oncogenic KRAS accelerates progression with varying histology.
Mouse acinar and endocrine cells initiate PanIN more readily than duct cells; histologically early PanIN cells can invade locally and disseminate.
Acinar-derived mouse tumours pass through ADM/PanIN, are less proliferative and have better organised collagen; duct-derived tumours bypass the PanIN stage.
PanIN precedes invasive cancer in genetically engineered mouse models, supporting the human PanIN sequence; ADM and atypical flat lesions were first described in mice.
The sources read do not describe KC or KPC mouse histology (mPanIN grades, murine PDA) in detail, and the names KC and KPC are not used.
